# Research basis and limits — 2026-10-28

This is a research-informed engineering and AI workflow suite, not an academically validated intervention. Author credentials alone are not evidence. Sources distinguish peer-reviewed empirical work, mathematical results, preprints, standards, and practitioner guidance. Source pages/abstracts were inspected for the stated claims; this is a targeted review, not a systematic literature review or replication. Not every recommendation was tested in these papers.

## Interpreting rules

- **Research finding:** bounded by the study population, task, model, and date. Association is not causation.
- **Standard / practitioner guidance:** a documented method or requirement, not proof of an optimal workflow.
- **Suite default / inference:** our operational choice; tune with local outcomes. Numerical limits are defaults unless a source and applicability establish otherwise.
- **Local requirement:** an adopted repository policy, user constraint, or applicable obligation. Preserve it until an authorized change; never quietly weaken it to pass an audit.

Separate observed evidence, inference, unknown, and not applicable. A documented policy is not an enforced control. A static skill check is not proof of runtime compliance. Historical Muse reports describe individual exercises, not whole-suite effectiveness.

## Evidence register

| ID | Primary source and kind | Finding or method | Boundary and application |
|---|---|---|---|
| R01 | Bacchelli & Bird (2013), [Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review](https://www.cabird.com/pubs/bacchelli2013eoc.pdf), ICSE empirical study | Review supports understanding and knowledge transfer as well as defect discovery. | Microsoft setting; no universal line-count limit. Review context and behavior. |
| R02 | Inozemtseva & Holmes (2014), [Coverage Is Not Strongly Correlated with Test Suite Effectiveness](https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~rtholmes/papers/icse_2014_inozemtseva.pdf), ICSE empirical study | Controlling suite size weakens the relationship between coverage and fault detection. | Studied Java systems and mutation-based effectiveness; coverage still identifies untested code. |
| R03 | MacCormack, Baldwin & Rusnak (2012), [Product and organizational architectures](https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/Research%20Policy%2041%20%282012%29%201309%E2%80%93%201324_c5c2350e-013c-4065-a2f9-d95eb32177d5.pdf), Research Policy comparative study | Organizational and software modularity are related in the examined matched products. | Not a deterministic law or proof that reorganization causes improvement. |
| R04 | Bird et al. (2011), [Don't Touch My Code!](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/dont-touch-my-code-examining-the-effects-of-ownership-on-software-quality/), ESEC/FSE empirical study | Expertise/ownership measures relate to quality in the studied systems. | Does not validate RACI or excluding newcomers. Route knowledgeable review and develop backup expertise. |
| R05 | Little (1961), [A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/opre.9.3.383), Operations Research mathematical result | Relates long-run average items, throughput, and time in a stable system. | Match boundaries and units; not a percentile forecast or an optimal utilization limit. |
| R06 | Flyvbjerg (2006), [From Nobel Prize to Project Management: Getting Risks Right](https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.3642), Project Management Journal; author manuscript | Reference-class forecasting uses outcomes from comparable projects. | Infrastructure examples do not calibrate software probabilities. Check comparability and calibration locally. |
| R07 | Edmondson (1999), [Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/13a7b031-0fdd-45ec-a7e0-2b80e2bc679f), Administrative Science Quarterly empirical study | Psychological safety is associated with learning behavior in 51 manufacturing teams. | Transfer to software incident practice is an inference, not proof of a postmortem template. |
| R08 | Forsgren et al. (2021), [The SPACE of Developer Productivity](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-space-of-developer-productivity-theres-more-to-it-than-you-think/), ACM Queue research framework | Productivity spans dimensions and cannot be represented by activity alone. | Framework, not a validated universal composite score. |
| R09 | Dow et al. (2010), [Parallel prototyping](https://doi.org/10.1145/1879831.1879836), ACM TOCHI experiment; publisher abstract inspected | Parallel alternatives improved outcomes in the studied design task. | No universal requirement for multiple polished UIs or fixed participant counts. |
| R10 | Amershi et al. (2019), [Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Guidelines-for-Human-AI-Interaction-camera-ready.pdf), CHI synthesis/validation | Guidelines address AI capabilities, errors, correction, and adaptation. | Contextual validation is still needed. Design recovery and control alongside the happy path. |
| R11 | Liu et al. (2024), [Lost in the Middle](https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.9/), TACL experiments | Information position affected retrieval and multi-document QA performance. | Older models, non-coding tasks; no universal context-size cap. |
| R12 | Yang et al. (2024), [SWE-agent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.15793), NeurIPS research paper | Agent-computer interface design affects navigation, editing, and testing performance. | Benchmark/model dependent. Prefer legible tool feedback and verification evidence. |
| R13 | Xia et al. (2024), [Agentless](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01489), research manuscript | Localization, repair, and validation supplied a competitive simple benchmark baseline. | Not evidence that agents never help. Compare added orchestration against a simple workflow. |
| R14 | Gloaguen et al. (2026), [Evaluating AGENTS.md](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11988v3), preprint v3, September 29 | Context files did not generally improve success in the studied settings and increased average inference cost. | Particular agents/models and repository tasks. Keep useful nonstandard instructions; evaluate additions, not a blanket shorter-is-better rule. |
| R15 | Becker et al. (2025), [AI and experienced developer productivity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089), randomized trial/preprint | Early-2025 AI increased task time in this experienced-developer sample despite perceived speedups. | Not a universal current effect. [METR's February 2026 update](https://metr.org/blog/2026-02-24-uplift-update/) reports selection/time-measurement problems in its follow-up. Measure local end-to-end outcomes. |
| R16 | Sculley et al. (2015), [Hidden Technical Debt in ML Systems](https://papers.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2015/hash/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Abstract.html), NeurIPS systems paper | Data dependencies, feedback, and configuration create system-level debt. | Not an LLM release standard. Version relevant dependencies and monitor beyond code tests. |
| R17 | Breck et al. (2017), [The ML Test Score](https://research.google/pubs/the-ml-test-score-a-rubric-for-ml-production-readiness-and-technical-debt-reduction/), IEEE Big Data practitioner research | Readiness spans data, models, infrastructure, and monitoring. | Industrial rubric; use applicable checks, not a universal score as a certificate. |
| R18 | Liang et al. (2023), [Holistic Evaluation of Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.09110), TMLR benchmark/framework | Standardized scenarios and multiple metrics expose trade-offs and coverage gaps. | Benchmark success does not validate a product. Use representative held-out cases. |
| R19 | Zheng et al. (2023), [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685), NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks | Judges approximate preferences but exhibit position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases. | Preference agreement is not functional correctness. Calibrate judges; prefer executable checks. |
| R20 | Greshake et al. (2023), [Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173), research paper | Instructions in retrieved data can redirect integrated applications. | Demonstrations do not quantify every deployment's risk. Test boundaries; enforce authority outside the model. |
| R21 | Kim et al., [Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.08296v3), preprint revised April 2026 | Across 260 configurations, six benchmarks, five architectures, and three model families, architecture-task fit changes benefits; tool-heavy tasks incur coordination overhead. | Moderate predictive fit; no universal optimal team size or suite speedup. Select workers by task structure and compare with solo. |
| R22 | Zhang et al., [AgentPrune](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.02506), research paper | Pruning spatial/temporal message edges reduced tokens in tested multi-agent frameworks. | Reported 28.1-72.8% reductions are benchmark-specific, not a forecast for hand-written routing. Remove redundant messages and rounds, then measure. |
| R23 | Zhang et al. (2025), [G-Designer](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/zhang25cu.html), ICML | Learned task-dependent communication graphs evaluated across six benchmarks, including HumanEval. | Short code benchmarks do not establish repo-scale gains; a learned graph model requires training/evaluation. Separate task dependencies from message routing. |
| R24 | Cemri et al. (2025), [Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657v3), empirical preprint | MAST classifies 14 failure modes; released data includes 1,600+ traces across seven frameworks. | Taxonomy development used 150 expert-guided traces. Repetition, stopping, misalignment, and verification motivate evals; this controller remains unvalidated. |
| R25 | Yu et al. (2026), [Multi-Agent Memory from a Computer Architecture Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.10062), position paper | Frames shared/distributed memory and consistency/access-control gaps. | Architectural argument, not measured performance. Version artifacts and reject stale evidence; do not treat shared summaries as ground truth. |
| R26 | Jaroslawicz et al. (2025), [How Many Instructions Can LLMs Follow at Once?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11538), NeurIPS 2025 benchmark | Accuracy falls as simultaneous instructions rise (best model 68% at 500); early instructions are favored at moderate density. | Keyword-inclusion task, not coding workflows. Budget rule count and put critical rules first. |
| R27 | Cognition, [Don't Build Multi-Agents](https://cognition.ai/blog/dont-build-multi-agents) (2025) and [Multi-Agents: What's Actually Working](https://cognition.com/blog/multi-agents-working) (2026), practitioner reports | Parallel writers make conflicting implicit decisions; agents contributing analysis while writes stay single-threaded works. | Vendor experience, not controlled studies. Supports one writer per coupled change. |
| R28 | Anthropic (2025), [multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), engineering report | Lead-plus-subagents beat single-agent by 90.2% on internal research evals; token use explained ~80% of BrowseComp variance. | Breadth-first research, not coupled coding; gains come with much higher token cost. |
| R29 | Huang et al. (2024), [LLMs Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01798), ICLR | Without external feedback, self-correction rarely fixes reasoning and can degrade it. | Reasoning benchmarks. Prefer executed checks and independent review over self-reread. |
| R30 | Hong et al. (2025), [Context Rot](https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot), Chroma technical report | Across 18 models, reliability degrades non-uniformly as input length grows, even on simple tasks. | Length and difficulty partly confounded. Retrieve just in time; keep context small. |
| R31 | Anthropic (2025), Effective context engineering for AI agents, engineering guidance | Treat context as finite: compaction, notes outside the window, just-in-time retrieval. | Practitioner guidance, not measured suite gains. |
| R32 | DORA (2025), [State of AI-assisted Software Development](https://dora.dev/research/ai), survey (~5,000 respondents) | AI amplifies existing strengths and dysfunctions; small batches matter especially with AI. | Associational survey data. |
| R33 | Husain and Shankar, [error analysis](https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/why-is-error-analysis-so-important-in-llm-evals-and-how-is-it-performed.html), practitioner guidance | Read real traces, note failures, group into a taxonomy, then write evals and calibrate judges. | Method guidance; trace counts are heuristics. |
| R34 | SkillWren benchmark round 2 (local, 2026), blinded review task | A rubric enforced as an explicit verification gate raised severity accuracy 6/8 -> 8/8 at ~5x fewer skill tokens. | One task, 8 seeded findings, one round; a hypothesis that body-level gates help, not a measured suite gain. |

## Standards and practitioner sources

- **P01:** [Google engineering practices](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/) — review guidance; response times/change sizes are conventions.
- **P02:** [MADR](https://adr.github.io/madr/) — decision rationale/format. [Scrum Guide 2020](https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html) — framework requirements, not universal laws.
- **P03:** [DORA trunk-based development](https://dora.dev/capabilities/trunk-based-development/) and [delivery metrics](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/) — research-informed practices; associations do not prove every cutoff causal.
- **P04:** SRE Workbook: [SLO alerting](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/), [example budget policy](https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/), [canary releases](https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/). Adapt examples to traffic, windows, and risk.
- **P05:** [NIST SSDF 1.1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final) and [SLSA 1.2](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/) — versioned frameworks. Neither establishes this suite's 7/30/90-day default. SBOMs and artifact signatures do not substitute for build provenance.
- **P06:** [Four Question Framework](https://github.com/adamshostack/4QuestionFrame) — threat-model method; ordinal scores are not quantitative risk predictions.
- **P07:** Testing and integration practice: Google Testing Blog ("Test Sizes", "Code Coverage Best Practices", "Flaky Tests at Google"), Cohn's test pyramid, Fowler's "The Practical Test Pyramid", Pact docs, [trunkbaseddevelopment.com](https://trunkbaseddevelopment.com/), Humble and Farley, *Continuous Delivery*, [SemVer 2.0.0](https://semver.org/), [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/). Practitioner guidance; ratios, CI durations, and branch ages are adjustable defaults.
- **P08:** Release and operations practice: Google SRE Book ch. 4, 8, 14-15 and Workbook ch. 2, 5, 10, 16; Hodgson, "Feature Toggles"; Unleash docs on flag debt; PagerDuty Incident Response docs; Allspaw, "Blameless PostMortems and a Just Culture" (2012). Example thresholds and deadlines are policy to adopt locally.
- **P09:** Design, security, and planning practice: Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011); Shostack, *Threat Modeling* (2014); OWASP ASVS and Top 10 for LLM Applications; PMI WBS Practice Standard; Wake's INVEST; Lawrence's story-splitting guidance. Methods, not measured outcomes.

## Maintenance

Each active skill links here with applicable IDs and operational implications. Load this register when assessing evidence or revising policy, not for every task. Re-check mutable specifications before claiming compliance. Re-run comparisons after changing instructions, models, tools, or retrieval. Publish task counts, configurations, raw results, and limitations; do not turn one audit into a suite rating.
